clips.text: The winter of 32 to 31 BC. Antony sails back to the Peloponnese and winters at Patrae.
clips.spoken: The winter of 32 to 31 BC. Antony sails back to the Peloponnese and winters at PAT-ree.

clips.text: He spreads his soldiers out, to guard the strategic points and secure provisions.
clips.spoken: He spreads his soldiers out, to guard the strategic points and secure provisions.

clips.text: His garrisons hold Corcyra. He holds Methone.
clips.spoken: His garrisons hold kor-SY-ruh. He holds meh-THOH-nee.

clips.text: We read this chain of posts as probably guarding the supply route from Egypt. That is our reading; the passage speaks only of guard and provisions.
clips.spoken: We read this chain of posts as probably guarding the supply route from Egypt. That is our reading; the passage speaks only of guard and provisions.

clips.text: Before spring 31 BC, Agrippa takes Methone by storm, and kills Bogud there.
clips.spoken: Before spring 31 BC, Agrippa takes meh-THOH-nee by storm, and kills BOH-gud there.

clips.text: From there he watches for the merchant ships, and raids the coasts of Greece.
clips.spoken: From there he watches for the merchant ships, and raids the coasts of Greece.

clips.text: Those were most likely grain ships from Egypt. That is our reading; the passage says only merchant ships.
clips.spoken: Those were most likely grain ships from Egypt. That is our reading; the passage says only merchant ships.

clips.text: In spring 31 BC, Octavian crosses the Ionian Gulf from Brundisium with his whole force.
clips.spoken: In spring 31 BC, Octavian crosses the Ionian Gulf from Brundisium with his whole force.

clips.text: His cavalry lands at the foot of the Ceraunian mountains.
clips.spoken: His cavalry lands at the foot of the Ceraunian mountains.

clips.text: He seizes Corcyra, abandoned by its garrisons, and occupies Toryne, in Epirus.
clips.spoken: He seizes kor-SY-ruh, abandoned by its garrisons, and occupies TOR-ih-nee, in Epirus.

clips.text: He camps on the high ground north of the strait, where Nicopolis later stood.
clips.spoken: He camps on the high ground north of the strait, where Nicopolis later stood.

clips.text: From Toryne he probably marched south to that camp. We have drawn the road; the sources give the places, not the march.
clips.spoken: From TOR-ih-nee he probably marched south to that camp. We have drawn the road; the sources give the places, not the march.

clips.text: Summer 31 BC. Agrippa takes Leucas, takes Patrae after beating Nasidius at sea, and later takes Corinth.
clips.spoken: Summer 31 BC. Agrippa takes LOO-kus, takes PAT-ree after beating nuh-SID-ee-us at sea, and later takes Corinth.

clips.text: Antony's forces lose men to disease and desertion.
clips.spoken: Antony's forces lose men to disease and desertion.

clips.text: Velleius puts it plainly: "from Antony to Caesar someone or other was deserting daily."
clips.spoken: Velleius puts it plainly: "from Antony to Caesar someone or other was deserting daily."

clips.text: Cut off from bringing in grain, Antony's provisions begin to fail.
clips.spoken: Cut off from bringing in grain, Antony's provisions begin to fail.

clips.text: Now to the battle itself.
clips.spoken: Now to the battle itself.

clips.text: The battle is fought on the morning of 2 September, 31 BC.
clips.spoken: The battle is fought on the morning of 2 September, 31 BC.

clips.text: Antony's fleet draws up its line a little outside the strait, and comes no further.
clips.spoken: Antony's fleet draws up its line a little outside the strait, and comes no further.

clips.text: Antony orders his ships to hold their position at the narrow mouth of the gulf.
clips.spoken: Antony orders his ships to hold their position at the narrow mouth of the gulf.

clips.text: Octavian keeps his ships about eight furlongs away, some one and a half kilometres, and waits a long time.
clips.spoken: Octavian keeps his ships about eight furlongs away, some one and a half kilometres, and waits a long time.

clips.text: Cleopatra's sixty ships lie behind the line.
clips.spoken: Cleopatra's sixty ships lie behind the line.

clips.text: Who commanded where? The sources disagree.
clips.spoken: Who commanded where? The sources disagree.

clips.text: Plutarch gives Antony the right wing, with Publicola; Coelius the left; Marcus Octavius and Marcus Insteius the centre. Octavian, he says, posts Agrippa on the left and keeps the right for himself.
clips.spoken: Plutarch gives Antony the right wing, with pub-LIK-oh-luh; SEE-lee-us the left; Marcus Octavius and Marcus in-STAY-us the centre. Octavian, he says, posts Agrippa on the left and keeps the right for himself.

clips.text: Velleius names Publicola and Sosius as commanders of Antony's fleet, without wings. For Octavian he gives the right to Lurius, the left to Arruntius, and full charge of the fight at sea to Agrippa.
clips.spoken: Velleius names pub-LIK-oh-luh and SOH-shee-us as commanders of Antony's fleet, without wings. For Octavian he gives the right to LOO-ree-us, the left to uh-RUN-shus, and full charge of the fight at sea to Agrippa.

clips.text: A modern summary, Wikipedia's, combines the two, and gives Antony's left wing to Sosius, which neither ancient passage we hold says.
clips.spoken: A modern summary, Wikipedia's, combines the two, and gives Antony's left wing to SOH-shee-us, which neither ancient passage we hold says.

clips.text: The map draws one arrangement only. It is a reconstruction, not any one source's.
clips.spoken: The map draws one arrangement only. It is a reconstruction, not any one source's.

clips.text: At the sixth hour, about midday, a wind rises from the sea, and Antony's men put their left wing in motion.
clips.spoken: At the sixth hour, about midday, a wind rises from the sea, and Antony's men put their left wing in motion.

clips.text: Plutarch says "the soldiers of Antony became impatient at the delay."
clips.spoken: Plutarch says "the soldiers of Antony became impatient at the delay."

clips.text: Octavian orders his right wing to row backwards, to draw them out of the gulf and the narrows.
clips.spoken: Octavian orders his right wing to row backwards, to draw them out of the gulf and the narrows.

clips.text: In the afternoon, Agrippa extends his wing to encircle the enemy. Publicola advances against him, and is cut off from the centre.
clips.spoken: In the afternoon, Agrippa extends his wing to encircle the enemy. pub-LIK-oh-luh advances against him, and is cut off from the centre.

clips.text: Antony's centre falls into confusion, engaging Arruntius.
clips.spoken: Antony's centre falls into confusion, engaging uh-RUN-shus.

clips.text: We have placed this on the northern side of the battle. The compass point is our reading, not the sources'.
clips.spoken: We have placed this on the northern side of the battle. The compass point is our reading, not the sources'.

clips.text: Then, suddenly, Cleopatra's sixty ships hoist their sails and make off through the midst of the fighting.
clips.spoken: Then, suddenly, Cleopatra's sixty ships hoist their sails and make off through the midst of the fighting.

clips.text: They take advantage of the wind, and make for the Peloponnese.
clips.spoken: They take advantage of the wind, and make for the Peloponnese.

clips.text: Cassius Dio says she turned to flight from the strain of waiting, and signalled her ships.
clips.spoken: Cassius Dio says she turned to flight from the strain of waiting, and signalled her ships.

clips.text: Velleius puts it on her: "Cleopatra took the initiative in the flight; Antony chose to be the companion of the fleeing queen rather than of his fighting soldiers."
clips.spoken: Velleius puts it on her: "Cleopatra took the initiative in the flight; Antony chose to be the companion of the fleeing queen rather than of his fighting soldiers."

clips.text: Panic, her initiative, or a planned breakout? Did she escape through a gap in the line? Historians still disagree, and the question stays open.
clips.spoken: Panic, her initiative, or a planned breakout? Did she escape through a gap in the line? Historians still disagree, and the question stays open.

clips.text: Antony leaves the fight in a five-oared galley, with only Alexas the Syrian and Scellius, and goes after her.
clips.spoken: Antony leaves the fight in a five-oared galley, with only Alexas the Syrian and SKEL-ee-us, and goes after her.

clips.text: Dio says he thought her ships fled from fear, not at her bidding, and so he followed.
clips.spoken: Dio says he thought her ships fled from fear, not at her bidding, and so he followed.

clips.text: The fleet left behind, it seems, has lost its commander.
clips.spoken: The fleet left behind, it seems, has lost its commander.

clips.text: But not its money. Dio says the money was still aboard the ships left fighting, and Octavian held back from fire to gain it.
clips.spoken: But not its money. Dio says the money was still aboard the ships left fighting, and Octavian held back from fire to gain it.

clips.text: Desertion, or a planned escape? That question, too, is still open.
clips.spoken: Desertion, or a planned escape? That question, too, is still open.

clips.text: With the fight still even, Octavian sends to the camp for fire.
clips.spoken: With the fight still even, Octavian sends to the camp for fire.

clips.text: His ships attack from many sides, with blazing missiles, torches, and pots of charcoal and pitch.
clips.spoken: His ships attack from many sides, with blazing missiles, torches, and pots of charcoal and pitch.

clips.text: Plutarch says Antony's fleet held out until the tenth hour, worn down by a rising sea. Three hundred ships are captured.
clips.spoken: Plutarch says Antony's fleet held out until the tenth hour, worn down by a rising sea. Three hundred ships are captured.

clips.text: On land, Antony's legions hold together for seven days, ignoring Octavian's messages.
clips.spoken: On land, Antony's legions hold together for seven days, ignoring Octavian's messages.

clips.text: Only then does Canidius run away by night, and the army goes over to Octavian without fighting.
clips.spoken: Only then does kuh-NID-ee-us run away by night, and the army goes over to Octavian without fighting.

clips.text: After the battle.
clips.spoken: After the battle.

clips.text: Antony is taken aboard Cleopatra's ship. He means to cross from Taenarum to Libya.
clips.spoken: Antony is taken aboard Cleopatra's ship. He means to cross from TEE-nuh-rum to Libya.

clips.text: Where they parted, the sources differ. Dio says they went as far as the Peloponnese together, and Cleopatra then hastened to Egypt.
clips.spoken: Where they parted, the sources differ. Dio says they went as far as the Peloponnese together, and Cleopatra then hastened to Egypt.

clips.text: Plutarch says Antony reached the coast of Libya, and sent her on into Egypt from Paraetonium.
clips.spoken: Plutarch says Antony reached the coast of Libya, and sent her on into Egypt from pa-ree-TOH-nee-um.

clips.text: Antony stays at Paraetonium until the news of Pelusium.
clips.spoken: Antony stays at pa-ree-TOH-nee-um until the news of peh-LOO-zee-um.

clips.text: Now, the end of the war.
clips.spoken: Now, the end of the war.

clips.text: Before Alexandria, Antony's fleet goes over to Octavian. Plutarch tells it as the crews' own choice; Dio says Cleopatra caused the ships to desert.
clips.spoken: Before Alexandria, Antony's fleet goes over to Octavian. Plutarch tells it as the crews' own choice; Dio says Cleopatra caused the ships to desert.

clips.text: His cavalry deserts, his infantry is beaten, and he retires into the city.
clips.spoken: His cavalry deserts, his infantry is beaten, and he retires into the city.

clips.text: Told that Cleopatra is dead, Antony wounds himself, and dies with her in the tomb.
clips.spoken: Told that Cleopatra is dead, Antony wounds himself, and dies with her in the tomb.

clips.text: Octavian drives into the city.
clips.spoken: Octavian drives into the city.

clips.text: The city fell, by the usual account, on 1 August 30 BC; no passage we hold gives the date.
clips.spoken: The city fell, by the usual account, on 1 August 30 BC; no passage we hold gives the date.

clips.text: Cleopatra dies. Octavian admires her spirit, and has her buried with Antony.
clips.spoken: Cleopatra dies. Octavian admires her spirit, and has her buried with Antony.

clips.text: Octavian now holds all power alone.
clips.spoken: Octavian now holds all power alone.
